Teaching With AI

Explore tools, guidance, and practical examples to help you use AI effectively and responsibly in your teaching.

Artificial intelligence can help educators streamline routine tasks, enhance communication and feedback, support instructional brainstorming, and create new opportunities for student engagement.

Human expertise and judgment remain at the center of teaching and learning. When used in course development, AI-generated content can provide a starting point for ideas and drafts, but it cannot replace disciplinary expertise, intentional course design, or professional judgment. Instructors remain responsible for ensuring that course materials, assignments, and teaching approaches advance learning objectives, respond to student needs, reflect disciplinary standards, and align with university policies.
When incorporating AI into your teaching, set clear expectations for student use, design learning experiences that promote critical thinking and authentic engagement, and help students understand AI's capabilities, limitations, and responsible use.

AI Tools for Instructors

Whether you're creating course materials, preparing lectures, providing feedback, or exploring new teaching strategies, the university offers AI tools to support your work. Choose institutionally supported tools whenever possible and follow course, privacy, and academic integrity expectations when using AI.

Creating a class policy
A policy does not have to be extensive, but it should provide clear guidance to students on how they may and may not use generative AI in your class. We urge instructors to permit the use of ChatGPT and other tools wherever appropriate but also to talk with students about why you are approaching things as you are.
Here are two examples. One is short. The other offers more explanation to students. The second version is from an editing class that Doug Ward, associate director of CTE, teaches. It can be easily adapted to nearly any discipline, though.
Brief version
You may use ChatGPT and other generative AI tools in this class in some instances. That includes generating ideas, outlining steps in a project, finding sources, getting feedback on your writing, and overcoming obstacles on papers and projects. Using those tools to generate all or most of an assignment, though, will be considered academic misconduct. If you are ever in doubt, ask. In your course work, you will be asked to explain in a reflection statement how you used any generative AI tools.

Guidance on the Use of Generative AI in Higher Education
Research
Policies governing AI use in research, including manuscript and grant preparation, continue to
evolve across federal agencies, journals, and institutions. Investigators, project staff, and
students are responsible for staying current on applicable policy and for critically assessing the
reliability of AI tools within the research context (NIH, 2023).
AI as an Author
Journals and research communities are in consensus that AI models cannot be listed as
authors. Authorship requires the capacity to take responsibility for submitted work, declare
conflicts of interest, and manage copyright and licensing, none of which an AI model can do
(COPE, 2023; Zielinski et al., 2023; Flanagin et al., 2023; Nature, 2023).
